The new 'Competition Model 2.0' lets scientists focus on the science idea first, cuts the wait time from 35 months to about 19.5 months, and opens the door wider so universities and smaller teams can take part. The result? More missions, more often, racing toward space.

news.title: 5 Things You Should Know About the 2026 Dakar Youth Olympics
What Is Aerocapture and How Could It Help Spacecraft Reach Mars?
news.excerpt: A California startup called Inversion is working with NASA to master a clever space trick: using a planet's atmosphere to grab a spacecraft and slow it down — all without burning extra rocket fuel.

news.title: Can Europe beat Starlink with its own super constellation?
news.excerpt: Ukraine relies on Elon Musk's Starlink network for battlefield communications, but when the service slows down, whole armies lose contact. Europe is racing to build its own satellite internet system — but its best alternative is still years away.

news.title: What happens when a mushroom makes you see tiny humans walking on your dinner plate?
news.excerpt: In parts of China and the Philippines, people eat a special wild mushroom called Lanmaoa asiatica for its savory flavor — but if it isn't cooked long enough, they start seeing dozens of tiny human figures climbing on their food, walking around furniture, and even swimming in their soup. Scientists have finally identified the mushroom responsible and discovered it does NOT contain any known psychedelic compounds like psilocybin — the chemical that causes its strange effects is a complete mystery.

news.title: How did NASA's OSIRIS-REx asteroid mission find organic building blocks from the dawn of the solar system?
news.excerpt: After a decade of surprising discoveries, NASA has wrapped up the OSIRIS-REx mission — but the spacecraft's journey continues onward to a new target: asteroid Apophis. Along the way, it brought back the largest asteroid sample in history from Bennu, filled with clues about how our solar system began.

news.title: How do spinning googly-eyed buoys and bird kites keep seabirds safe from fishing nets?
news.excerpt: Off the coast of Cornwall, engineers are testing colorful 'scarecrow' devices — spinning buoys with big googly eyes and soaring bird-of-prey kites — that warn seabirds away from fishing nets, cutting accidental catches by up to 71%.

news.title: Scientists discover a hidden crystal patchwork that has fooled superconductor research for 40 years?
news.excerpt: For 40 years, scientists assumed a family of high-temperature superconductors had the same crystal structure all the way through. New 3D X-ray imaging now shows they are a patchwork of different atomic arrangements stitched together by boundaries hundreds of times wider than expected — and those boundaries may silently weaken superconductivity.

news.title: Why is NASA racing to put humans back on the Moon — and what did the latest update reveal?
news.excerpt: NASA wants to return humans to the Moon faster than ever — and it just gave a new update on the timeline for the big comeback.

news.title: When will SpaceX and Blue Origin land on the Moon? NASA lays out the race
news.excerpt: NASA has laid out a step-by-step timeline for SpaceX's Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon to prove they can carry astronauts to the Moon — with key tests happening through 2027 and 2028.

news.title: Can a 15-minute water trick fix carpal tunnel without surgery?
news.excerpt: A simple injection that uses fluid to free a squeezed nerve may help people avoid carpal tunnel surgery — and it only takes about 15 minutes.

news.title: How did scientists build a 3D cloak that hides things from heat vision?
news.excerpt: Scientists have built the world's first 3D thermal invisibility cloak that can hide objects from infrared cameras while keeping them safe from extreme heat and cold.

news.title: How did astronauts' hearts handle six months in space — and will they be OK on Mars?
news.excerpt: A study of 13 astronauts found that daily exercise helped their hearts adapt to months in weightless space and pass a simulated test of Mars' gravity — making the red planet look a little more reachable.

news.title: How a Giant Bridge Over the Highway Is Letting Colorado's Wildlife Cross Safely
news.excerpt: A 200-foot-wide wildlife overpass spanning Interstate 25 in Colorado has cut animal-vehicle collisions by 91% in its first 10 months — proving that when we build bridges for nature, everyone wins.

news.title: Why do we always pick 'safe' over 'dangerous'? Scientists find a hidden bias in human language
news.excerpt: Scientists have discovered that the words we choose — whether in stories, tweets, or conversation — lean heavily toward safety over danger. This hidden bias, found by analyzing billions of words, could change how we study language and teach computers to understand us.

news.title: How were two brown bears saved from Tiny cages? A 5-Year Rescue Across Three Countries
news.excerpt: For five years, two brown bears named Bu and Tyapa waited in tiny Russian cages. One had been forced to perform in a circus, the other was kept in a box too small to stand. In August 2026, after delays caused by war and transport bans, they finally arrived at Wild Ireland sanctuary in Ireland — where they are learning to be bears again.

news.title: How Did Scientists Discover a Pac-Man Enzyme That Gobbles Plastic?
news.excerpt: Scientists have found a special enzyme — nicknamed the 'Pac-Man enzyme' — that bacteria use to chew through plastic. The discovery shows how nature is already fighting pollution, one tiny bite at a time.

news.title: How did scientists fix the hidden glitch that slows down quantum computers?
news.excerpt: Scientists in Japan found that a tricky physics effect called the AC Stark shift was making errors when many quantum bits were controlled at the same time. They beat the error with a clever calibration trick — bringing practical quantum computers one step closer.

news.title: Why does Antarctica have a new channel named after a reporter?
news.excerpt: A stretch of icy water in Antarctica is now called the Amos Channel, after BBC science reporter Jonathan Amos. The waterway only appeared when a chunk of ice connecting two islands broke apart.

news.title: How did flare ribbons help scientists solve the mystery of hidden solar explosions?
news.excerpt: The Sun throws the Solar System's biggest tantrums — solar flares that blast energy billions of times stronger than a volcano. But some of these explosions hide in plain sight. New research shows that bright 'ribbons' of light flashing on the Sun's edge are the footprints of magnetic energy that has just snapped and reconnected, revealing the secret mechanics of the Sun's most powerful blasts.

news.title: How did a bipartisan U.S. bill try to end the wildlife trade in sloths?
news.excerpt: After dozens of sloth deaths at a Florida tourist attraction, U.S. Representatives introduced the bipartisan SLOTHS Act to ban the import of wild sloths — protecting these gentle tree-dwellers from a trade that kills up to 90% of captured animals.

news.title: How did Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry become the first human to fly to space — after death?
news.excerpt: On October 22, 1992, the space shuttle Columbia carried more than cargo to orbit — tucked inside astronaut James Wetherbee's personal kit was a small container of Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry's ashes. It was humanity's first 'space burial' and a dream Roddenberry never got to fulfill in life.

news.title: How did removing rats and pigs bring an island's wildlife roaring back to life?
news.excerpt: On a tiny Pacific island in Samoa, removing invasive rats and pigs let the forest grow back, baby birds start nesting, and native wildlife return — showing what teamwork between communities and conservationists can do.

news.title: What is the golden tree coral that glows underwater off Costa Rica?
news.excerpt: Scientists exploring underwater mountains off Costa Rica found a bright yellow coral so unusual that they had to invent a brand-new family name for it. What makes this 'golden tree of the stars' so special — and why did its genes refuse to agree?

news.title: How did two caged brown bears travel 5 years and 2 continents to find a forest home in Ireland?
news.excerpt: After spending years in cramped cages in Russia, two brown bears named Bu and Tyapa finally reached a forest sanctuary in Ireland — a journey made possible by over 100 volunteers and two major world conflicts that nearly stopped it.

news.title: How did 20% of Switzerland's glacier ice disappear in just five years?
news.excerpt: Switzerland's glaciers lost 5% of their ice volume in a single year, and nearly 20% of the country's glacier ice has vanished since 2021 — an alarming sign of how quickly our planet's frozen giants are disappearing.

news.title: Why did a Russian spy satellite play cat-and-mouse with a commercial US spacecraft?
news.excerpt: A Russian reconnaissance satellite named Kosmos 2612 followed a commercial US radar satellite called ICEYE-X36 through low Earth orbit — getting as close as just a few meters at one point in a silent, non-consensual game of orbital chicken.

news.title: What are the five spooky Halloween skywatching targets this October?
news.excerpt: Ready for a spooky stargazing adventure? Five Halloween skywatching targets — the Pleiades, the Demon Star, the Sea Monster, lunar spiderwebs, and Halloween fireballs — are glowing in October's night sky.

news.title: How did scientists figure out the best way to save the Amazon rainforest?
news.excerpt: A new Science journal study analyzed 3 million hectares of Amazon rainforest and found that protecting the trees already standing — especially from fires and logging — does more for both biodiversity and carbon storage than planting new ones.

news.title: How did seabirds bounce back on the Isle of Man — and why are sewage and storms still a challenge?
news.excerpt: On the Isle of Man, a whole-island UNESCO Biosphere reserve has brought back nesting seabirds and native juniper — but sewage still flows into the sea and young salmon keep disappearing. A decade in, the island's first-ever 'State of the Biosphere' report shows both wins and worries as UNESCO decides next summer whether to keep the island's special status.

news.title: 5. How Did a 700-Year-Old Chinese Mural End Up at the Met — and Why Did a Chinese Art Institute Spend 3 Years Copying It?
news.excerpt: A 700-year-old Medicine Buddha mural from a Chinese temple was carefully copied by artists over three years, revealing a 2-centimeter tilt in the Buddha's head that museum conservators had missed.

news.title: How did a Minnesota man stop a runaway school bus full of kids?
news.excerpt: When a school bus rolled down a Minnesota street with its doors wide open and no one controlling it, a quick-thinking bystander named Ebro Ahmed ran toward danger, jumped onto the moving bus, and brought it to a safe stop — saving 19 children and earning a $1,000 reward.

news.title: How did Giovanni Cassini spot Saturn's 'yin-yang' moon Iapetus 355 years ago?
news.excerpt: On October 25, 1671, Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered Iapetus, Saturn's peculiar moon with one half as dark as night and the other as bright as snow. Using only a 17th-century telescope, Cassini noticed something strange — Iapetus seemed to appear and disappear depending on which side of Saturn it sat. The mystery would puzzle astronomers for over 300 years.

news.title: How do rare Moon rocks that fall from space fill gaps in our story of the Moon?
news.excerpt: Some of the best Moon rocks never came from a spacecraft — they are meteorites that were blasted off our nearest neighbor eons ago and rained down on Earth, bringing us pieces of the Moon we never visited.

news.title: How did Spinosaurus become a part-time fish hunter in the ancient seas?
news.excerpt: A new Yale University study shows that Spinosaurus — the giant dinosaur with a crocodile-like snout — spent most of its life hunting underwater, joining a list of land animals that returned to the sea.

news.title: How did scientists reach the ultimate quantum limit right on a crystal surface?
news.excerpt: Scientists created an ultra-clean crystal surface so still that individual molecules sitting on it kept their quantum properties for the maximum time physics allows — the 'Fourier limit' — a first for molecules anchored to a surface.

news.title: How did a 2,500-year-old king earn the world's first human rights badge?
news.excerpt: A 29-foot bronze statue of Cyrus the Great now stands in Atlanta's Pardis Park, honoring the ancient Persian king historians call the world's first champion of human rights.

news.title: How did scientists discover a meteor hit happened 100 million years later than they thought?
news.excerpt: Scientists used tiny zircon crystals to figure out that a giant meteorite that crashed into Oklahoma happened 100 million years later than they originally thought — and it might be linked to one of Earth's biggest mass extinctions!

news.title: How did scientists find a soil compound that kills bad gut bacteria without harming the good ones?
news.excerpt: Scientists discovered that argyrin B, a compound made by soil-dwelling myxobacteria, can selectively kill harmful gut bacteria while sparing the beneficial microbes that keep our digestion healthy — a major step toward more targeted antibiotics.

news.title: What are HawkEye 360's signal-hunting satellites, and how does Rocket Lab put them in orbit?
news.excerpt: Rocket Lab launched three new Hawk satellites for HawkEye 360 on October 23, 2026 — special spacecraft that hunt invisible radio signals across Earth and help track ships, spot jamming, and map radio chatter from space.

news.title: How a super-powered laser microscope could let scientists see inside living cells for the first time
news.excerpt: Scientists have built a new kind of electron microscope that uses the world's most intense laser to make tiny proteins and cellular structures visible for the first time — potentially revealing how molecular machines work inside living cells.

news.title: How One Kenyan Business Owner Taught Us About Trust and Teamwork
news.excerpt: When Kenyan food creator That Girl Boina returned from a holiday, a customer's message revealed a problem that taught her a big lesson about trust, teamwork, and protecting your dreams.

news.title: What makes a narwhal's tusk twist like a double helix?
news.excerpt: Scientists used giant X-ray lights to peer inside the narwhal's legendary tusk and discovered it is built like a double helix — two spirals twisting in opposite directions, like a natural piece of rope.

news.title: How does growing plants in space help us care for Earth?
news.excerpt: NASA astronaut Luke Delaney is busy tending to plants aboard the International Space Station, testing how microgravity changes the way life grows — and what that tells us about tending our own planet from up above.

news.title: Why did Zhu Xi's ideas become the backbone of China's scholar exams for 800 years?
news.excerpt: Zhu Xi, born 896 years ago on October 18, 1130 in present-day Shaowu, China, transformed Confucian thought with his commentaries on the Four Books and his philosophy of qi and li — shaping the minds of scholars for over eight centuries.

news.title: Who runs the world's most southerly post office — and why is a penguin the boss?
news.excerpt: For five months each year, a postmaster named George Clarke leaves his home in Bristol to sort letters at the world's most southerly post office — on a tiny Antarctic island where about 1,000 gentoo penguins are permanent neighbors.

news.title: Europe's ExoMars Reaches Mars: The Orbiter That Survived and the Lander That Fell
news.excerpt: On October 19, 2016, the European Space Agency's ExoMars mission touched down at the Red Planet. The Trace Gas Orbiter went into orbit, while the Schiaparelli lander's attempt to land ended in a dramatic crash.

news.title: How did a volcanic eruption 27 million years ago create a new U.S. national park?
news.excerpt: Chiricahua, known as the 'Land of Standing-Up Rocks,' is now America's 64th national park. The stunning rock spires formed from a volcanic eruption 27 million years ago and have been protected since 1924.

news.title: How did X-ray scientists discover that uranium crystals can survive for decades underground?
news.excerpt: Tiny uranium oxide crystals trapped in soil from a 1986 nuclear accident have retained their original atomic structure for nearly 40 years — revealed by scientists using a technique called synchrotron X-ray diffraction that rotates each particle like a tiny gem in a focused X-ray beam.

news.title: Could the first exomoon be hiding in a strange star system far away?
news.excerpt: Astronomers using the Very Large Telescope in Chile may have spotted the first moon beyond our Solar System — but it's not orbiting a planet. It circles a brown dwarf, a 'failed star' millions of times dimmer than the Sun. If confirmed, it would rewrite how we think about moons and worlds.

news.title: What is SpaceX's mysterious Starfall capsule, and why did it fly again?
news.excerpt: SpaceX's Starfall capsule flew for only the second time ever on its Bandwagon-5 rideshare mission — carrying tiny space factories and dozens of small satellites back to Earth.

news.title: The Moon That Looks Like Yin-Yang: How Cassini Discovered Iapetus
news.excerpt: On October 25, 1671, Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini spotted a strange, shiny speck near Saturn. It turned out to be Iapetus — a moon so oddly half-dark and half-bright that astronomers still call it Saturn's 'yin-yang' moon.

news.title: How does a hidden protein switch turn cells into fat-burning machines?
news.excerpt: Scientists found a protein called Mitch that acts like a switch — flip it off and cells burn more fat and stop making new fat cells. The discovery could lead to new ways to fight obesity that don't just suppress appetite.

news.title: How did cryo-electron microscopy reveal why statins cause muscle pain?
news.excerpt: Scientists used cryo-electron microscopy to see, almost atom by atom, how statin molecules latch onto a muscle cell's calcium channel and hold it open — causing the calcium leak that leads to muscle pain.

news.title: What happened when a cabin leak warning flashed during NASA's Artemis II moon mission?
news.excerpt: A mysterious warning light just 15 minutes before the critical engine burn could have changed everything. Here is how NASA's crew and mission control quickly figured out it was a false alarm and safely sent the astronauts on their historic journey around the Moon.

news.title: 10 Things You Need to Know About India's Chandrayaan-1, the Moon Mission That Found Water Ice
news.excerpt: On October 21, 2008, India's space agency ISRO launched Chandrayaan-1 — its very first mission to the moon. This clever spacecraft not only proved India could explore deep space, but it also made a groundbreaking discovery: water ice hidden in the moon's shadowed craters.

news.title: What Was Zond 8 and Why Was It the Last Soviet Moon Mission?
news.excerpt: On October 20, 1970, the Soviet Union launched Zond 8 — a robotic spacecraft that flew around the Moon and returned home safely. It was the final mission in a program that tested spacecraft for future cosmonaut trips to the Moon.

news.title: How did a single module transform the International Space Station from a cramped shed into a spacious home?
news.excerpt: On October 23, 2007, the space shuttle Discovery launched the Harmony module — a 14-foot-wide connecting hub that doubled the International Space Station's living space and became the gateway for future international laboratories.

news.title: Why do tropical trees breathe at night — and how does it help them survive drought?
news.excerpt: Some tropical trees have a special trick: they open their pores at night, store carbon dioxide as a sour juice, and keep them closed all day. Scientists found that an ancient genome-duplication event gave different Clusia trees different versions of this water-saving superpower.

news.title: How Does the James Webb Telescope Reveal Baby Stars Hidden in Cosmic Dust?
news.excerpt: NASA's James Webb Space Telescope has pierced the dusty veil of NGC 7129, a stellar nursery 3,300 light-years away in the constellation Cepheus. Webb's infrared eyes revealed over 130 baby stars — some less than 1 million years old — that were completely invisible to previous telescopes.

news.title: How did AI read millions of Reddit posts to find hidden drug side effects?
news.excerpt: Scientists taught an AI to scan nearly 150,000 Reddit posts from people taking an unapproved weight-loss drug. The AI found something surprising: users reported increased appetite — the opposite of what the drug is supposed to do.

news.title: Can Solar Panels Help Grapes Grow Better?
news.excerpt: Scientists in Italy found that wine grapes grown under solar panels grew bigger, healthier, and needed less water — a clever way to help both energy and farming.

news.title: How were zebra sharks almost lost forever? Scientists rewilded them with a bold new plan
news.excerpt: For the first time ever, scientists have rewilded an endangered shark species. In Indonesia's Raja Ampat, 82 captive-bred zebra shark pups were released into a protected sanctuary — a breakthrough that could help save sharks from extinction worldwide.

news.title: NASA's asteroid Bennu samples reveal a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
news.excerpt: Tiny grains of dust from asteroid Bennu are teaching scientists that our Solar System was a much bigger mixing bowl than anyone thought — material from both the hot inner region and the icy outer region swirled together near Jupiter's newborn gravity.

news.title: Japan launches historic mission to bring home samples from Mars' mysterious moon
news.excerpt: Japan's MMX spacecraft has launched on a five-year journey to land on Phobos — one of Mars' tiny moons — and return the first-ever soil samples from the Red Planet's moon system to Earth by 2031.

news.title: How a Tiny Imperfection in a Crystal Revealed a Big Quantum Mystery
news.excerpt: Scientists figured out how a small defect inside a diamond or silicon chip changes its energy when light hits it — a discovery that could lead to better quantum sensors and computers.

news.title: Why do we always say 'safe' — scientists discover a hidden bias in human language?
news.excerpt: For over 70 years, scientists thought word meaning was organized by emotion — how positive or negative a word feels. Now, a team at the University of Vermont has discovered that language actually orbits around three deeper ideas: power, danger, and structure. Their tool, the 'ousiometer,' analyzed billions of words and found a surprising pattern: humans use 'safe' words far more than 'dangerous' ones.

news.title: How Do Black Holes Launch Giant Space Jets — and Why Do Some Have Two Disks?
news.excerpt: When a supermassive black hole swallows gas, it sometimes fires twin jets of energy into space. New X-ray images show these jets are powered by an inner hot disk sitting inside a cooler outer disk — a two-layer arrangement that solves a decades-old puzzle.

news.title: How did Brazil give millions of workers an extra day off each week?
news.excerpt: Brazil's Senate voted 75-1 to end the 6-day workweek, cutting the maximum workweek from 44 to 40 hours and guaranteeing two paid days off — the first change to labor hours since the 1988 Constitution.

news.title: SpaceX's Falcon 9 Slows Down as Starlink Satellites Soar from California
news.excerpt: A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket blasted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base on Oct. 23, carrying 27 new Starlink satellites. It was the rocket's 116th flight of 2026 — but as SpaceX shifts to its bigger Starship rocket, Falcon 9 launches are happening less often than before.

news.title: How will NASA test the Artemis 3 moon-lander in space?
news.excerpt: NASA just laid out a step-by-step plan for the Artemis III moon-lander test flight — a practice run in low-Earth orbit that will bring astronauts one step closer to walking on the Moon's south pole.

news.title: Can a private telescope find alien worlds? Lazuli aims to try
news.excerpt: Scientists have picked 27 alien worlds for the world's first private space telescope, Lazuli, to study using a special instrument that blocks starlight.

news.title: Are Giant Black Holes the Missing Dark Matter?
news.excerpt: Scientists have long wondered if dark matter — the invisible stuff that holds galaxies together — might be made of very heavy black holes. But a new study shows that stupendously large black holes cannot be a major part of dark matter.

news.title: Why are some monkey brains smooth instead of wrinkly — and what it teaches us about our own?
news.excerpt: Common marmosets are tiny monkeys with almost perfectly smooth brains. Scientists discovered that their brain-builder cells divide more slowly and grow simpler than ours, producing fewer neurons and far fewer folds — helping explain how small changes at the cellular level led to big differences in primate brains.

news.title: What is Jio Platforms' record-breaking IPO in India?
news.excerpt: A huge Indian telecom company called Jio Platforms is going public with what could become India's biggest-ever stock market sale, aiming to raise billions to expand internet access and new technologies across the country.

news.title: Can tiny robot triangles build tomorrow's giant space telescopes?
news.excerpt: Space is full of big ideas, but rocket fairings are small. A new design lets self-folding triangular modules link themselves together in orbit — adjusting their own shape as they go.

news.title: Why did Europe's Space Rider crash during its drop test — and what happens next?
news.excerpt: Europe's first reusable spacecraft prototype had a rough landing during a test — but scientists say it's all part of learning how to build better flying machines.

news.title: How did an ancient sea creature navigate with a tiny magnetic compass 97 million years ago?
news.excerpt: Tiny magnetic fossils from 97 million years ago may be the oldest evidence of an animal using Earth's magnetic field like a built-in GPS — a sophisticated navigation system that could help explain how modern birds and fish evolved their own magnetic sense.

news.title: Can scientists save the banana from disaster before it's too late?
news.excerpt: The banana on your breakfast table could one day vanish — but scientists are racing to breed a super-banana that can fight back.

news.title: How could we detect mirror life if it existed?
news.excerpt: Scientists have a plan to spot a hypothetical 'mirror life' — organisms built from reversed molecules — before they ever exist. The trick? Light that knows which way is left.

news.title: SpaceX Aims to Catch Both Pieces of Its Giant Starship Rocket
news.excerpt: SpaceX's next Starship test flight could be the first time a rocket is caught by its launch tower in TWO pieces at once — boosting both stages straight back to the pad for reuse.

news.title: How can DNA testing help save England's rarest tree?
news.excerpt: Conservationists are using DNA testing to help bring back the black poplar — one of the UK's rarest native trees — along the Thames Valley.

news.title: What did the Sunrise-III balloon find in the Sun's hidden magnetic web?
news.excerpt: A balloon-borne telescope called Sunrise-III floated 35 km above Earth in 2024 and revealed that even the Sun's 'quiet' regions are laced with a surprisingly intricate web of magnetic threads — not the smooth, simple canopy scientists expected.

news.title: Will Wales be the first place to say goodbye to ugly power lines?
news.excerpt: Wales is planning to ban new steel pylons and bury power cables underground instead — a move that could change how we get electricity across the countryside.

news.title: What Do Flare Ribbons Tell Us About the Sun's Hidden Explosions?
news.excerpt: Solar flares are among the Sun's most powerful explosions, but they happen behind the Sun's bright glare. Scientists are now using flare ribbons — glowing streaks that act like a flare's footprints — to see what these explosions really look like.

news.title: How Did the First Mammals Learn to Swallow — and Why That Made Room for Big Human Brains?
news.excerpt: A tiny 165-million-year-old Jurassic predator reveals the anatomical breakthrough that let early mammals swallow safely — the step that eventually made big, smart brains like ours possible.

news.title: Why was Ukraine's Starlink internet slow for a week — and how did it get fixed?
news.excerpt: Ukraine's military relies on SpaceX's Starlink satellite network to fly drones and stay in touch on the battlefield. Recently the connection slowed to a crawl for a week — drones lost signal above 100 mph — before the system was restored to full speed.

news.title: How did an orphaned gorilla named Lulingu learn to be a mother in the wild — and why is her baby a milestone for an endangered species?
5. How MIT built a paper-thin robot that swims using living muscle cells
news.excerpt: MIT engineers built a robot just as thin as a sheet of paper that swims by flapping two tiny fins — each powered by a layer of living muscle cells thinner than a strand of hair. The cells twitch when zapped with light, meaning no batteries or motors are needed.

news.title: How did a V-2 rocket take the first photo of Earth from space?
news.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a captured German V-2 rocket flew higher than anyone had ever gone before — and its motion-picture camera snapped the very first pictures of our home planet from the blackness of space.

news.title: Why is the ground doing a strange dance beneath a volcano that looms over 2 million people?
news.excerpt: Satellites have discovered that the ground around Nicaragua's Masaya volcano is moving in opposite directions — one part sinking while another rises — as two hidden magma reservoirs behave very differently.

news.title: How kids in Ecuador are turning beach trash into science treasure
news.excerpt: Children on Ecuador's coast are collecting cigarette butts, plastic bottles, and other debris — then logging every item into a science database that helps researchers track ocean pollution.

news.title: How did one cell become a whole body — and can we read its secret diary?
news.excerpt: Scientists used a DNA 'typewriter' to trace every cell in a developing mouse embryo back to its very first division. The result is a detailed family tree showing how cells choose their jobs — and why some turn into brain while others become skin.

news.title: How a Boat Trip on Lake Kariba Unearthed a Lost-World Dinosaur
What is NASA sending to the Moon aboard a rover named FLIP?
news.excerpt: A California space company is sending a rugged supercomputer and AI computer to the Moon's south pole this year — riding on a rover named FLIP.

news.title: 5 Spooky Halloween Skywatching Targets: Medusa's Eye and Ghostly Meteors
news.excerpt: As Halloween approaches, five spooky but kid-safe skywatching targets light up the October night sky — the winking Demon Star, the ghostly Pleiades, the sea monster Cetus, spiderweb moon craters, and the Halloween fireballs from comet Encke's debris trail.

news.title: Why does your aging brain trade memory for wisdom?
news.excerpt: Growing older doesn't just mean forgetting where you left your keys. A new way of understanding the aging brain suggests that, over the years, your mind quietly reshapes itself — relying a little less on a tiny seahorse-shaped region that records every detail, and a little more on the outer layer that pulls out the big picture and the wisdom you've gathered.

news.title: Are white dwarfs really white? Scientists find some glow pink, yellow, and even green
news.excerpt: White dwarfs are supposed to be white — but new research shows that leftover pieces of shattered planets in their atmospheres can make them glow pink, yellow, or even green. About 1 in 30 white dwarfs may look very different from their name.

news.title: How a $10 chip could turn your watch into a mini lab
news.excerpt: Cambridge scientists built a tiny optical sensor that costs about $10 and fits on a fingertip — it can read your blood sugar without needles and tell the difference between coffee, flour, and plastic.

news.title: Why did ancient seekers chase long life? 6 lessons science actually learned
news.excerpt: People have searched for long, healthy lives for thousands of years. Some quests ended badly, but every mistake taught science something new about the body, health, and how to live longer.

news.title: NASA's asteroid Bennu samples reveal a 4.5-billion-year-old secret about how our Solar System formed
news.excerpt: Tiny space rocks stolen from the dawn of the Solar System are telling us where Earth's water came from and how a young Jupiter stirred the cosmic recipe book.

news.title: Does fish oil really keep your brain sharp?
news.excerpt: A careful two-year study found that omega-3 fish oil pills did reach the brain, but they did not boost memory or protect thinking skills in older adults — suggesting food-first nutrition may beat supplements.

news.title: Why did Blue Planet III keep the cloudy, 'imperfect' shots? It's all real!
news.excerpt: The BBC's new ocean documentary leaves in cloudy water and floating debris on purpose — to prove every animal is real and no AI fakery snuck in.

news.title: Can a clever machine clean toxic algae from our lakes before it makes us sick?
news.excerpt: Hot summer weather turns some lakes green and pea-soup thick with toxic blue-green algae. Now a scientist's idea — born after watching his own child's favorite park close — could give nature a hand.

news.title: Can a 240-year-old pond in Cornwall be swimmable again?
news.excerpt: A historic bath house pond built in the late 1700s on the Antony Estate in Cornwall is being restored so people can swim in it again — bringing a piece of living history back to life.

news.title: How does a spider turn a silk web into a catapult that catches ants?
news.excerpt: A newly discovered Australian spider has built a spring-loaded silk trap that flings itself — or its web — at aggressive green tree ants, making it the first spider known to let its prey trigger its own capture.

news.title: Where do October's shooting stars come from? Halley's Comet left a trail of dust 6 trillion miles long
news.excerpt: Every October, Earth plows through a vast trail of dust shed by Halley's Comet, setting the stage for the Orionid meteor shower — one of the most reliable sky shows of the year.

news.title: How a ghostly, eyeless snail learned to live in a dark Chinese cave
news.excerpt: Deep inside a limestone cave in southern China, scientists found a tiny, see-through snail that has never needed eyes — it has lived its whole life in complete darkness, surviving on diatoms and the faint glow of underground rock.

news.title: How did Australia's desert turn into a rainbow — and what satellites saw from space?
news.excerpt: After unusually heavy rains, Australia's red outback erupted into a carpet of wildflowers — the brightest bloom in nearly 20 years. NASA satellites captured the dramatic transformation from space.

news.title: How do tiny snakes roll four times faster than they slither?
news.excerpt: Tiny Southeast Asian snakes called dwarf reedsnakes can roll across the ground at up to four times their normal slithering speed — all while keeping their heads perfectly still so they never lose sight of where they are going.

news.title: 5. Your Brain Has a Secret Post Office — and It Sends Messages to Just the Right Spots
news.excerpt: Deep inside your brainstem sits a tiny blue spot that acts like a smart postal service — sending targeted chemical messages to specific brain regions instead of broadcasting to everyone.

news.title: How did rescuers save 66 workers when a Nairobi skyscraper suddenly collapsed?
news.excerpt: When an 18-storey building under construction suddenly collapsed in Nairobi's Eastleigh district, emergency crews raced to pull people to safety — rescuing 66 of 67 workers and searching for seven people trapped in shops below.

news.title: Is Mars still alive? The giant canyon that proves our red neighbor is still changing today
news.excerpt: Scientists have found that Valles Marineris — the Solar System's largest canyon, stretching nearly 4,000 km across Mars — is still actively reshaping the Red Planet today, with fault lines deep beneath the canyon slipping and triggering marsquakes.

news.title: How do astronauts earn science's highest honor? Artemis II crew wins the Hawking Medal
news.excerpt: The four Artemis II astronauts traded places with movie stars and rock legends when they received the Stephen Hawking Medal for science communication at Starmus VIII.

news.title: What hidden magnetic web did a balloon telescope find above the Sun?
news.excerpt: A balloon-borne telescope called Sunrise-III floated 35 km above Earth in 2024 and spotted delicate, thread-like magnetic structures woven through the Sun's 'quiet' regions — a hidden web that may help explain how the Sun's atmosphere stays hot.

news.title: What does the edge of a sparkling spiral galaxy look like from 37 million light-years away?
news.excerpt: NASA's Hubble Space Telescope captured a stunning side-on view of NGC 1827, an intermediate spiral galaxy 37 million light-years away, revealing its star-studded disk and dusty lanes.

news.title: The moon is shrinking — 10,000 cracks show us exactly how much it has gotten smaller
news.excerpt: A new study found over 10,000 fault scarps on the moon's surface — cracks that form when the moon's interior cools and its rocky shell contracts. The data shows our nearest celestial neighbor has shrunk by about 148 feet over the past 400 million years.

news.title: Why Denmark said goodbye to mink farms — and what it means for the animals
news.excerpt: Denmark, once the world's biggest mink fur producer, is banning mink farming. Here is why the government changed its mind and what happens to the farms and the animals.

news.title: Is one side of this alien world a blistering hot desert — and the other a cool breeze?
news.excerpt: NASA's James Webb Space Telescope used a new 'transmission strings' technique to map an exoplanet's atmosphere — and discovered the planet is shaped like an egg, with one side 650 degrees hotter than the other.

news.title: What ancient plants are surviving in England's coldest valley — and how are kids helping save them?
news.excerpt: In Upper Teesdale, England, a special group of plants that have lived since the last Ice Age are getting help from a new £65,000 conservation project — collecting seeds, training volunteers, and planting them in the high fells.

news.title: 10 Forgotten Math Heroes Who Secretly Built the Modern World — and How You Use Their Ideas Every Day
news.excerpt: You use their inventions every single day — your phone screen rotates thanks to matrices, your GPS works because of curved-space math, and every chart you see owes a debt to one Renaissance mathematician's bookkeeping trick.

news.title: How does a black hole's dinner disk power its cosmic fire hoses?
news.excerpt: Supermassive black holes launch twin jets of energy, but their outer disks shouldn't be able to generate the strong magnetic fields those jets need. New X-ray and radio data show the inner disk swaps into a hotter, thicker form that does the job.

news.title: When hailstones the size of marbles fall from the sky — what happened in Phoenix?
news.excerpt: A rare autumn storm dropped golf ball-sized hail on Phoenix, Arizona, smashing car windshields and house windows. Here is how hail forms and why some storms produce such heavy ice.

news.title: What Makes Glass a Good Conductor of Heat? The Surprising Role of Sound
news.excerpt: Glass may seem like an insulator, but scientists have discovered that the speed of sound traveling through silicate glass is the dominant factor controlling how well it conducts heat — a finding that could help design better smartphone screens and electronic components.

news.title: Can a Soy Compound Shield Your Brain From Too Much Salt?
news.excerpt: A soy-derived compound called LPC70 may help protect the brain from the hidden harms of too much salt.

news.title: How did a black hole get kicked out of its galaxy — and end up swinging back like a pendulum?
news.excerpt: When two supermassive black holes merge at the heart of a galaxy, the collision can fire the new black hole away from the center — not into space, but swinging back and forth like a pendulum. New statistical evidence from a huge survey of quasars confirms this cosmic dance actually happens.

news.title: How did a baby walrus survive alone on an Alaskan beach? A community came together to save him
news.excerpt: A 5-month-old Pacific walrus calf named Annautaq was found alone on a remote northern Alaska beach, guarded by scavengers. A network of researchers and rescuers worked together to reunite him with care at SeaWorld Orlando.

news.title: How did an octopus cheat death — and star in Blue Planet III?
news.excerpt: A new clip from Blue Planet III shows an octopus that ventured too far from home, found itself in a hunter's jaws — and slipped away with a trick few creatures could match.

news.title: Saudi Arabia joins the search for alien signals from the night sky
news.excerpt: Saudi Arabia has installed two LaserSETI optical detectors in the ancient desert city of AlUla, becoming the first Asian site in a global network that listens for laser signals from distant civilizations.

news.title: How NASA's Dragonfly 'Dragon' Did Its First Practice Flight on Saturn's Weird Moon
news.excerpt: NASA's Dragonfly drone robot just completed its very first practice flight — but instead of flying on a distant moon, it stayed close to home at a Maryland laboratory to test all its systems before the real journey to Saturn's moon Titan.

news.title: What happens when a total solar eclipse darkens ancient Egypt?
news.excerpt: On August 2, 2027, a total solar eclipse will turn day into night over Luxor, Egypt — the longest total eclipse of the 21st century, nicknamed the 'Eclipse of the Century.'

news.title: What are the critical tests that the Griffin-1 lunar lander must pass before its Moon mission?
news.excerpt: The Griffin-1 lunar lander has passed a gauntlet of extreme tests at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, simulating the vibrations, temperatures, and sounds of launch and landing — all before its first trip to the Moon's south pole later this year.

news.title: Supernovae helped light up the early universe — but not how scientists thought
news.excerpt: For decades, astronomers assumed that supernova explosions were the main engines clearing paths for the ultraviolet light that ended the cosmic Dark Ages. New observations suggest young stars did most of the work first, before the first supernovae even went off.

news.title: Why are Switzerland's glaciers melting so fast?
news.excerpt: Switzerland's glaciers are losing ice faster than ever. In just five years, nearly 20% of the country's glacier ice has vanished — and some glaciers have disappeared entirely. Here is why the mountains are turning bare.

news.title: When a humpback whale mother stayed beside her stillborn calf — what it tells us about whale feelings
news.excerpt: Scientists watching off Australia's Gold Coast observed a humpback whale mother remaining beside her deceased newborn for days — offering a rare glimpse into how these gentle giants may experience loss and love.

news.title: How Solar Orbiter Traced Mysterious Magnetic Kinks Back to the Sun
news.excerpt: For the first time, ESA's Solar Orbiter has traced a giant magnetic switchback — an S-shaped kink in the solar wind — all the way back to its origin near a coronal hole on the Sun, revealing how these mysterious features form and affect space weather.

news.title: How did a test camera take one of the most stunning photos of space?
news.excerpt: A smaller engineering camera at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory captured the Seagull Nebula in incredible detail, showing us what the future of astronomy looks like.

news.title: What happened when oil from a tanker washed up on UAE beaches?
news.excerpt: Satellite pictures track an oil spill from a damaged tanker in the Strait of Hormuz as it spreads along the United Arab Emirates' northern coastline.

news.title: How did a dark-energy telescope spot a comet 1.3 billion km from Earth?
news.excerpt: The ESA Euclid telescope went to space to study dark energy by photographing distant galaxies. Instead, it discovered its very first comet — C/2026 S1 — proving the best discoveries sometimes come from happy accidents.

news.title: Did farmers accidentally set off tsunamis in an Italian lake 900 years ago?
news.excerpt: On Jan. 3, 1117, an earthquake struck northern Italy so hard that Lake Garda and Lake Iseo overflowed their banks. Now researchers say centuries of farming on the slopes made the landslides that triggered the flood waves even worse — and the same danger could return today.

news.title: A coral reef hidden for 60 years was thought dead — so what did scientists find when they looked again?
news.excerpt: More than 60 years after scientists concluded a deep-water coral reef off Benin was probably dead, a team returned with modern cameras and found it alive and bustling with fish.

news.title: What giant-clawed 'unconquered warrior' dinosaur hid in a museum drawer for 100 years?
news.excerpt: A fossil skull fragment discovered on England's Isle of Wight over 100 years ago has finally been recognized as a brand-new species of feathered dinosaur — Invictibellatrix amberina, a small but fierce predator with curved claws up to 20 cm long.

news.title: Why should I stockpile and what will I need?
news.excerpt: The UK government says every household should keep three days' of easy supplies — water, food, and a few handy extras — so families can ride out storms, power cuts, or other surprises.

news.title: Why did the U.S. Secretary of State visit a small Indian refinery town?
news.excerpt: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio made an unusual choice on his recent trip to India — he skipped the capital, Delhi, and headed straight to Jamnagar, home to the world's largest oil refinery. The reason? America's need for refined fuel ahead of upcoming elections.

news.title: How did Danish beach plastic pellets trace back to a river in England?
news.excerpt: Tiny plastic pellets called nurdles — the raw material for making plastic bottles and bags — spilled from the River Tyne in July and washed up nearly 400 miles away in Denmark by September. Scientists tracked them across the North Sea.

news.title: How did a giant ancient volcano fill back up with molten rock?
news.excerpt: Deep beneath Japan, one of Earth's most powerful supervolcanoes is slowly rebuilding its underground magma reservoir — 7,300 years after one of the largest eruptions in history.

news.title: What are 27 alien worlds teaching us about a private space telescope?
news.excerpt: A new private space telescope called Lazuli is being built with a 3-meter mirror and a special instrument to study alien worlds by the light they reflect off their stars — and researchers have picked 27 glowing gas giants as its very first targets.

news.title: How a nationwide bird count turned every Australian into a citizen scientist?
news.excerpt: Australia's annual Aussie Bird Count asks anyone outside for 20 minutes to tally the birds they see — turning everyday walks into data that helps conservationists track how bird populations are faring across the continent.

news.title: Why does Earth's center of mass keep shifting — and how does NASA find it?
news.excerpt: Earth's center of mass drifts by a few millimeters every season as water, ice, and air shift around the planet — and NASA scientists now track those tiny movements with laser-ranging satellites and GPS.

news.title: Why is October's Moon called the Hunter's Moon?
news.excerpt: Every October the full Moon gets a special name. Here is why it is called the Hunter's Moon, why it shines for so long, and what makes it look so big near the horizon.

news.title: Why are we here at all — and could a ghost particle be the answer?
news.excerpt: The Universe should have made equal amounts of matter and antimatter — but it didn't, and that imbalance is what lets stars, planets, and us exist at all. Now a new study argues that heavy, short-lived neutrinos may be the hidden key that tipped the balance.

news.title: Webb's new photo of star nursery NGC 7129 shows baby stars in stunning detail
news.excerpt: NASA's James Webb Space Telescope has captured a new infrared image of NGC 7129 — a stellar nursery 3,300 light-years from Earth where more than 130 baby stars younger than 1 million years old are shining through dusty gas clouds.

news.title: Could a tiny crustacean really become a fish's living tongue?
news.excerpt: Scientists have confirmed that the tongue-eating louse — a tiny crustacean called Cymothoa exigua — is the only known parasite that can completely replace an entire organ in its host, stepping in as a living replacement for a fish's tongue.

news.title: Could Earth's next magnetic flip be linked to the planet's biggest die-offs?
news.excerpt: Every few hundred thousand years Earth's magnetic poles swap places. Fresh evidence from a 3.75 million-year-old rock core suggests the most unstable patch of that magnetic history lines up with the biggest mass extinctions — but scientists still can't prove the two are truly linked.

news.title: How removing rats and pigs gave a tiny island's wildlife a second chance
news.excerpt: On Nu'utele Island in Samoa, a team of conservationists, community members, and even a rugby star removed invasive rats and pigs — and within a year, native birds are nesting again, seedlings carpet the forest floor, and a land crab unseen for decades has returned.

news.title: 10 Ways Coconut Oil Could Power Your Next Flight — and Other Uses for the Miracle Nut
news.excerpt: Chemists in Japan turned leftover coconut oil into a jet-ready biofuel that burns cleaner than standard kerosene, showing how waste from one industry can fuel another — and maybe your next airplane trip.

news.title: Who keeps the lights on in winter? The grid operator's big job
news.excerpt: Britain's electricity network is run by a single team that has to make sure every home has power all winter. Here is how they balance wind, sun, and demand so the lights stay on.

news.title: How did sharks learn to eavesdrop on the ocean? Their hearing reaches 250 feet underwater
news.excerpt: Scientists discovered that blacktip sharks can detect low-frequency sounds from up to 250 feet away — and figure out where the sound is coming from.

news.title: Why do mother bats' hearts race when they hear their own babies' cries?
news.excerpt: In a dark cave roosting with hundreds of other bats, a mother must find her own babies by sound alone. Now scientists have measured what happens inside her body when she does — her heart beats faster, but only for her own pups.

news.title: How citizen scientists are watching the coastline change — one photo at a time
news.excerpt: A simple cradle that holds your phone + a camera app is helping scientists track how beaches grow and shrink across 21 countries — and anyone can join in.

news.title: How did Typhoon Champi become 2026's mightiest storm — and why is El Niño feeding it?
news.excerpt: Typhoon Champi grew into a Category 5 super typhoon — the strongest storm on Earth this year — with winds of 185 mph. A record-breaking El Niño in the Pacific pumped warm water into its path, giving it the energy to spin faster and faster.

news.title: How do animals live inside a cave with no light or eyes? China's ghostly cave snail shows us
news.excerpt: Deep inside a dark cave in southern China, scientists found a tiny, see-through snail that has no eyes at all — and it may already be running out of time.

news.title: Can a shark learn to swim back home? The tale of Bukangi the canal shark
news.excerpt: A three-metre dusky shark named Bukangi became a star in Busan, South Korea after getting stuck in a canal — and the whole city cheered as rescuers tried to guide her back to sea.

news.title: What do 2,884 exploding stars tell us about how the Universe grows?
news.excerpt: A record collection of 2,884 'standard candle' supernovae suggests that dark energy — the invisible force pushing the cosmos apart — may be weakening over time.

news.title: How did phosphorus keep Earth's oxygen flowing after the Great Oxygen Event?
news.excerpt: About 2.3 billion years ago, Earth's atmosphere gained its first lasting breath of oxygen. But a mystery remained — how did oxygen stay abundant enough for life to thrive over millions of years? The answer lies in an ancient recycling system driven by phosphorus in the oceans.

news.title: How a British astronaut surprised a classroom with a video from space
news.excerpt: A real astronaut sent a surprise video message to primary school kids in Plymouth — and they couldn't believe their eyes.

news.title: What happens when a hurricane runs out of warm water and turns into a wind monster?
news.excerpt: Hurricane Isaias ran out of warm ocean water and transformed into an extratropical cyclone — a comma-shaped 'bomb' storm that sent 205 km/h winds screaming past Iceland, all captured from space by NASA's NOAA-21 satellite.

news.title: What does JWST's new peek inside Orion reveal about baby stars?
news.excerpt: The James Webb Space Telescope sees through dusty clouds in Orion's stellar nursery to catch baby stars shooting out high-speed jets.

news.title: Where do those S-shaped kinks in the solar wind come from? Solar Orbiter traced them to the Sun
news.excerpt: A kink in the Sun's outflow of charged particles has been traced back to hot magnetic loops on the solar surface, confirming how magnetic reconnection shapes the solar wind and space weather.

news.title: 5 Secrets Hiding in Elizabeth I's Angriest Letters
Why did New York ban horse-drawn carriages — and what happens to the horses and drivers?
news.excerpt: New York City Council voted to ban horse-drawn carriage rides in Central Park starting in June 2028, ending a 160-year-old tradition after a teen tourist's tragic fall and decades of safety concerns.

news.title: How did a giant 1-metre scorpion stalk ancient Britain 415 million years ago?
news.excerpt: Scientists have re-identified fossils sitting in museum drawers for over 150 years as the largest known scorpion — Praearcturus gigas — a creature the size of a large dog that prowled ancient Britain long before trees existed.

news.title: Why are peat fires in Indonesia so dangerous — and what makes them hard to put out?
news.excerpt: Peat fires in Indonesia burn underground and create toxic haze that crosses borders, but the special spongy ground where they start makes them incredibly hard to extinguish.

news.title: How did a 50-foot snake rule ancient India 47 million years ago?
news.excerpt: Scientists have identified a massive 47-million-year-old snake named Vasuki indicus from western India — one of the longest snakes ever to slither the Earth, measuring up to 50 feet from head to tail and rivaling the legendary Titanoboa.

news.title: Why did Meta have to pay a record $25 billion — and what it means for your online privacy
news.excerpt: A U.S. judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion for misleading people about how their data is used — the largest penalty of its kind.

news.title: How long is the wait for a US green card — and why does it matter so much?
news.excerpt: Millions of people around the world hope to live and work in the United States with a green card. For highly skilled Indian tech workers, the wait can stretch for decades — what makes the line so long?

news.title: What makes hailstones grow so big?
news.excerpt: A rare hailstorm dumped golf-ball-sized ice on Phoenix, Arizona. Here is the simple science behind how frozen raindrops grow into bouncing ice marbles.

news.title: How did our Milky Way's two disk layers form — and when did the thin one appear?
news.excerpt: New Gaia satellite data reveals our Milky Way's disk flattened in two steps — a fast squeeze about 10.8 billion years ago then a slow calm that built the home of our Solar System.

news.title: Why are honey bees chasing away their wild cousins — and why does it matter?
news.excerpt: Honey bees are pushing wild bumblebees, solitary bees, and hoverflies away from flowers — and scientists say climate change could make the pushing even worse.

news.title: Why are marmoset brains smooth while human brains are wrinkled?
news.excerpt: Tiny brain-building cells grow and divide at different speeds in marmosets vs. humans — and those slow changes add up to a smooth brain instead of a heavily folded one.

news.title: Is that really Venus, or is it the Sun? This weekend Venus slips behind our closest star
news.excerpt: Starting this weekend, Venus — Earth's sister planet — slides behind the Sun from our sky view. It's a rare moment called 'inferior conjunction,' and you can still follow it online even when it disappears from sight.

news.title: 10 quiet math geniuses who secretly made your phone, plane, and game console work
news.excerpt: Matrices, probability, and abstract algebra sound like school stuff — but the brilliant but forgotten minds behind them built the invisible math that runs every photo, flight, and video game today.

news.title: Why is the Moon still shrinking? Space scientists find clues in cliff-lined fault scarps
news.excerpt: The Moon may look unchanged from millions of years ago, but new measurements show it is actually still cooling — and as it cools, it slowly shrinks, building tiny cliffs and causing moonquakes that future astronauts need to watch out for.

news.title: Did Van Gogh paint a real night sky? Scientists may have found the exact date
news.excerpt: One of the world's most famous paintings may have captured a real night sky — and a new study says scientists have finally figured out the exact date it was painted.

news.title: Why can't I just sit here? Starbucks' new China rule explained
news.excerpt: Starting today, Starbucks cafes in China require you to buy something to use their seats. Here's why the world's second-biggest coffee chain made the change.

news.title: How did scientists discover a whole new penguin species hiding in plain sight?
Why are the Iguazu waterfalls rushing at 10-times their normal power?
news.excerpt: A rain-soaked October in South America — linked by scientists to this year's Super El Niño — has sent the Iguazu River surging over the border between Argentina and Brazil at roughly ten times its usual flow.

news.title: Why do UK summers feel like ovens, and why is air-con still rare?
news.excerpt: Older UK homes were built to hold heat in, not push it out. During heatwaves the solid brick walls act like thermal batteries, storing the day's heat and radiating it back all night — turning a sunny afternoon into a sleepless, sweaty ordeal and pushing cities several degrees hotter than the countryside.

news.title: How can a dying coral come back just by touching a healthy one? A touch for 5 days is enough
news.excerpt: Bleached corals — ghostly white and close to dying — can fully recover in just seven weeks after touching a healthy, genetically identical coral for as little as five days. Stanford scientists found that brief contact is enough to pass beneficial algae back into the damaged coral and restart its recovery.

news.title: What is the Jackdaw gas field — and why is it in the news?
news.excerpt: The UK government has approved output from a new North Sea gas field called Jackdaw. Here is what that means — and what it might do to your energy bills.

news.title: How does Mars grow a 1,800-kilometre cloud — and why won't it stick around?
news.excerpt: Every Martian summer morning, a thin white cloud unfurls west of the giant Arsia Mons volcano, stretching nearly 1,800 km before fading — and a new study says it forms by a process once thought to exist only in textbooks.

news.title: How a giant bridge over a highway cut animal crashes by 91%?
news.excerpt: A 200-foot-wide wildlife bridge over Interstate 25 in Colorado has slashed vehicle-animal collisions by 91%, proving that when roads and nature cross the same space, a little concrete can save a lot of lives.

news.title: How Perseverance learned to drive itself across Mars on the road to a record
news.excerpt: Perseverance broke the far-driving record on Mars — but the real hero is brainy autopilot software that lets the rover think while it drives.

news.title: How Do Viruses Build Themselves Without a Blueprint?
news.excerpt: Tiny virus particles can assemble their protective shells using only simple trial-and-error rules — no worker drones, no architect, just proteins that keep trying until they get it right.

news.title: The lost dinosaur hidden in a drawer for 40 years
news.excerpt: A fossil dug up in Antarctica in 1985 spent four decades tucked away in a drawer, mistaken for a marine reptile, before a curator realized it was the very first dinosaur bone ever found on the frozen continent.

news.title: How a group of Caltech students turned rocket experiments into 90 years of space history
news.excerpt: In October 1936, Caltech students fired rockets in a dry riverbed in Pasadena — unknowingly founding the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Ninety years later, JPL is building interstellar probes, lunar drones, and helicopters that fly on Mars.

news.title: What happened when a 160-meter asteroid hit the North Sea and made a 330-foot tsunami
news.excerpt: About 43 to 46 million years ago a 160-meter-wide asteroid slammed into the North Sea, blasting a crater 3 km wide and sending a tsunami over 100 meters high crashing across the waves. New evidence has finally settled a 20-year-old debate about the mysterious Silverpit Crater.

news.title: Why are birds more afraid of women than men — and what does it mean for city birds?
news.excerpt: In cities across Europe, urban birds consistently fly away sooner when a woman approaches than when a man does — and scientists have no idea why. A new study of 37 bird species and over 3,000 encounters reveals the same surprising pattern from the Czech Republic to Spain, leaving researchers puzzled about what the birds are noticing.

news.title: Can we really un-break plastic? A new way to recycle acrylic glass
news.excerpt: Researchers in Switzerland found a clever trick to take old acrylic plastic — the kind in car lights and display cases — apart into its original building blocks, so it can be made into new plastic again without the huge heat old methods needed.

news.title: How did a hidden crater 700 meters under the North Sea get there — and what does an ancient asteroid tell us?
news.excerpt: Scientists have confirmed that the Silverpit Crater deep under the North Sea was carved by a 160-meter asteroid that struck 43 to 46 million years ago, after more than two decades of scientific debate.

news.title: Which period-drama details look too strange to be true — but really happened?
news.excerpt: Period dramas on TV and film show tiny teacups, frequent fainting, and people who never smile — but what looks like Hollywood exaggeration is often real history. Here are 10 everyday details from costume dramas that historians confirm really happened.

news.title: What happens when zoo lions eat like wild cats — whole prey, feasts, and fasts?
news.excerpt: Zoo lions given whole animal carcasses on a feast-and-fast schedule — spaced about nine days apart — spent nearly three times longer eating, tore and manipulated their food more naturally, and settled into a rhythm of intense feeding, deep rest, and gradual activity that mirrors wild lions.

news.title: A magic fabric blanket that triples strawberry harvests — and keeps bugs away without chemicals
news.excerpt: A special knitted fabric called Plant Armor, draped like a blanket over strawberry plants, boosted harvests by 3.56 times in North Carolina field tests while keeping insects out and cutting chemical pesticides.

news.title: Dame Judi Dench and her secret superpower: turning setbacks into stories
news.excerpt: Oscar-winning actress Dame Judi Dench, 91, says her eye condition stopped her from reading and performing — but her seven-decade career is full of stories that show how curiosity and humor win every time.

news.title: How Scientists Use X-ray Echoes to Map Black Holes at MIT
news.excerpt: At MIT's Kavli Institute, Professor Erin Kara uses X-ray 'echoes' to map the violent regions around black holes, helping us understand how these cosmic monsters grow and change.

news.title: How Strangers Helped an 86-Year-Old Finish His 62-Foot Boat
Why does Western Australia have a giant spider-shaped crater visible from space?
news.excerpt: A giant ancient impact crater in Western Australia looks like a spider when seen from space — and new satellite photos show its eight legs spreading across the red earth.

news.title: How much helium did the Big Bang create in its first 5 minutes?
news.excerpt: Scientists have measured how much helium was forged in the Universe's first five minutes with three-times better precision — using pristine 'time capsule' galaxies that have barely changed since the dawn of time.

news.title: When your brain guesses before you even see it
news.excerpt: Modern scientists now describe the brain as a prediction machine — and that idea is echoing back to a theory Sigmund Freud sketched more than 130 years ago, when he suggested the mind constantly fills in the blanks before reality arrives.

news.title: How did octopuses become so smart? Their DNA folded into a brand-new shape
news.excerpt: Octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish are masters of disguise and problem-solving. Now scientists say their super-smart brains may owe their evolution to a massive reshuffling of how their DNA folds inside cells — a 3D genome reorganization 500 million years ago that wired up new connections between genes.

news.title: Can Airbnb hosts still make guests strip beds and wash dishes?
news.excerpt: Airbnb has updated its global house rules so hosts can no longer ask guests to do chores like stripping beds, washing dishes, or taking out trash — but they can still set seven standard rules plus reasonable requests.

news.title: How did an 18th-century queen use King Arthur to prove she belonged on the throne?
news.excerpt: Queen Caroline of Ansbach was born in Germany. To make her family feel British, she built a cottage linked to King Arthur — turning an old legend into a PR story for the whole kingdom.

news.title: How did removing a dam bring salmon back to a river for the first time in 100 years?
news.excerpt: A century after the Elwha Dam silenced the river, salmon are swimming upstream again — and a tribe is reclaiming 1,100 acres of the land that was flooded for over 100 years.

news.title: Why are drought fires turning the sky over New Guinea a thick white-gray?
news.excerpt: Strong El Niño has dried out New Guinea's savannas and grasslands. Human-set fires are spreading across the unusually parched landscape, sending smoke visible from satellites and stirring up air-quality concerns for nearby communities.

news.title: Why can't humans make the sugar that's hiding in their burger?
news.excerpt: A sugar called Neu5Gc lives in beef and lamb but not in our own bodies. Humans lost the ability to make it millions of years ago -- and eating it may quietly spark inflammation linked to type 2 diabetes.

news.title: How did AI find a hidden 'secret door' in 70% of the world's websites — and fix it before hackers could?
news.excerpt: An AI system spotted critical security bugs in PHP — the language behind 7 in 10 websites — that had been hiding for over a decade. Security teams raced to patch them before bad actors could exploit them.

news.title: Why do weight-loss drugs sometimes leave skin looking loose?
news.excerpt: Weight-loss drugs that mimic a natural gut hormone help people lose weight fast — but when you drop pounds quickly, your skin sometimes can't bounce back, and that is changing how beauty companies make their products.

news.title: How does a galaxy act like a cosmic magnifying glass, and what is Hubble checking for the Roman telescope?
news.excerpt: NASA's Hubble Space Telescope is snapping images of gravitational lenses — where a foreground galaxy bends and magnifies light from a more distant galaxy — so that the new Roman Space Telescope can study them even better.

news.title: Can 4 minutes of daily exercise keep you strong as you grow?

news.title: How did a rock travel 90 kilometers into Earth?

news.title: How Japan's MMX mission will grab a piece of Mars' moon Phobos and bring it home

news.title: What happens to water when the pressure is 2 million times Earth's?
news.excerpt: Deep inside ice giants like Uranus and Neptune, water ice doesn't behave the way we expect — under 2 million times Earth's atmospheric pressure, it loses its molecular symmetry and becomes something entirely stranger than frozen H2O.

news.title: Why do we name big storms — and how does Storm Austen brew?
news.excerpt: A patch of low pressure coming in from the Atlantic is being called 'Storm Austen' before it even arrives. Here is why the wind spins up so fast — and how forecasters pick the name.

news.title: How did Indonesia protect 4 million acres of rainforest in one big decision?
news.excerpt: Indonesia decided to stop clearing 4.4 million acres of rainforest, swamps, and peatlands for rice and sugar farms — saving a habitat home to orangutans, proboscis monkeys, and clouded leopards instead.

news.title: How scientists built a lightning-fast laser to peer inside living cells
news.excerpt: A new laser-powered microscope at UC Berkeley can reveal tiny cell structures that were once invisible, helping scientists watch the hidden machinery of life in stunning detail.

news.title: Why do Appalachian mountain stories vanish under science? 5 legends solved
news.excerpt: People have told stories in the Appalachian Mountains for centuries. But some of these 'ghost' tales have down-to-Earth explanations — from sick deer to headlight trickery.

news.title: Is your morning coffee sneaking in 40% more calories? The creamer culprit scientists found
news.excerpt: Americans drink about the same amount of coffee as 18 years ago, but each cup now packs almost 40% more calories — and sugar is not the culprit. Non-dairy creamer has quietly taken over as the leading source of added coffee calories.

news.title: Why is the universe's first green star glowing ghostly green — and what its color reveals
news.excerpt: Astronomers found the first star that would actually look green to human eyes — a dense 'white dwarf' glowing green because of sodium in its atmosphere.

news.title: What strange cargo did SpaceX deliver to the Space Station this week?
news.excerpt: A SpaceX Dragon capsule docked with the International Space Station carrying more than just food and socks — its cargo bay held 3D heart tissue, brain organoids, materials for an artificial retina, and glass that only forms in zero gravity.

news.title: Why does your brain guess what happens next — and how Freud figured it out 130 years ago?
news.excerpt: Your brain is constantly guessing what comes next, then checking if it was right. Modern neuroscience has a name for this — but psychoanalyst Sigmund Freud was describing the same thing over a century ago.

news.title: 1,000 feet of cliffs on Mars: What's Curiosity's mystery layer on Mount Sharp?
news.excerpt: NASA's Curiosity rover has sent back a stunning new panorama from the slopes of Mount Sharp on Mars — a view of mysterious, wind-carved cliffs that scientists are racing to reach before 2027.

news.title: How did one island bounce back? Killing rats and pigs lets Samoa's native wildlife return
news.excerpt: When invasive rats and pigs were removed from Nu'utele Island in Samoa, native plants grew back, birds started nesting again, and even a land crab returned. Here is why taking away just two animals can bring an entire island back to life.

news.title: Is the Arctic losing its ice fortress?
news.excerpt: Satellites watching Earth since 1978 show the Arctic Ocean's floating ice cap is shrinking in both winter and summer — and what used to be thick, old ice is turning into thin, young ice that melts away each year.

news.title: 3 ghostly nebulas hiding in Cassiopeia that only show up with a special filter
news.excerpt: A new image from NASA's APOD shows the faint dust clouds of IC 59 and IC 63 — the 'Ghosts of Cassiopeia' — glowing red from a nearby bright star, plus three brand-new blue 'phantoms' lit up by a rare oxygen filter.

news.title: What if Tesla cars and SpaceX rockets joined the same team?
news.excerpt: Elon Musk — who runs both Tesla electric cars and SpaceX rockets — said he is thinking about merging the two companies into one giant tech team.

news.title: World's Oldest Shipwreck Found Off Turkey — 4,700-Year-Old Cargo Still Inside
news.excerpt: Archaeologists exploring the seafloor near Kekova Island in Turkey discovered a 4,700-year-old shipwreck — the oldest ever found — carrying amphorae that still held traces of their original cargo.

news.title: How a Laser 'Broom' Paints 3D Maps of Earth from Space — Without Any Moving Parts
news.excerpt: NASA's CASALS instrument uses rainbow light — not spinning mirrors — to sweep laser pulses across Earth, creating seamless 3D maps of forests and terrain in one pass.

news.title: Why Antarctic Sea Ice Flipped From Record Highs to Record Lows in Just a Decade
news.excerpt: For decades Antarctic sea ice grew a little each year. Then in 2015 the trend flipped, and 2026 brought the third-lowest winter maximum on the satellite record — scientists aren't sure if this is a short blip or a lasting shift.

news.title: Why are red squirrels thriving on Jersey but vanishing from the rest of England?
news.excerpt: Red squirrels are vanishing across England, yet on one small island they run, leap, and chatter in the trees — and people are fighting to keep them safe.

news.title: How a UK estate found 5,242 species — even during a drought
news.excerpt: At Wimpole Estate in Cambridgeshire, England, conservationists recorded more than 5,000 different plants and animals over just six years — including rare bats, newts, and birds — even as southern England faced its worst drought in decades. The secret? Working with nature, not against it.

news.title: How NASA's newest rocket engine test fired up for the Moon
news.excerpt: NASA just fired its most powerful rocket engine for 500 seconds — the same length of a real launch — as it prepares to send astronauts back to the Moon on the SLS rocket.

news.title: Why do pilot whales chase killer whales? The ocean's gentlest giants fight back
news.excerpt: Long-finned pilot whales are not just gentle social whales — they actively chase, mob, and even mimic the calls of killer whales, the ocean's top predator, in a rare case of a prey species standing its ground.

news.title: How NASA's new helicopter blades could fly 25x farther on Mars
news.excerpt: NASA's Ingenuity helicopter proved flight on Mars was possible. Now a new blade design could let the next generation of Mars helicopters fly 18.7 kilometers in a single trip — 25 times farther than Ingenuity ever managed.

news.title: Are there hidden black holes wandering near our Solar System?
news.excerpt: New Gaia satellite data hints that lonely stellar-mass black holes may be drifting through the nearby interstellar clouds, but the search so far has come up empty.

news.title: The Doomsday Predicted for Nov. 13, 2026 — Why the Scientists Were Wrong
news.excerpt: In 1960, scientists predicted humans would hit 'infinity' on Nov. 13, 2026 — squeezed to death by overpopulation. Their math looked brilliant. Then birth rates changed the story.

news.title: How NASA took to the sky at a football game
news.excerpt: NASA's Inspiration Tour brought a supersonic flyover and a space exhibit to a college football game in Alabama — meeting fans where they are.

news.title: What happens to your gut bugs when you swap sugar for sweetness?
news.excerpt: Scientists tested 39 popular sweeteners against 25 types of gut bacteria in the lab — and most of them shifted the balance of tiny microbes that keep our tummies happy.

news.title: 5 reasons smoky peat fires turn the sky over Borneo a rusty orange
news.excerpt: Each year in Southeast Asia, dry-season fires light up forests and swamps across Indonesian Borneo. The flames are mostly hidden underground, burning through layers of ancient peat, and the smoke they make travels thousands of miles across the ocean.

news.title: How did fuel leak into Wales' River Taff and hurt the fish?
news.excerpt: A fuel leak from a GE Aerospace repair site sent kerosene flowing nearly 2.5 miles down Wales' River Taff, leaving dead fish in its wake and teaching us why even small leaks can ripple into big trouble for rivers.

news.title: How did NASA's Roman Space Telescope get sharper focus than engineers expected?
news.excerpt: NASA's newest space telescope, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, is already working better than anyone planned — its main camera is delivering pictures nearly 30% sharper than predicted, after engineers nudged a mirror by just 1/16th of a human hair's width.

news.title: 10 famous musicians who grew to regret the songs that made them famous
news.excerpt: Some artists spend their whole lives running from one song. Here are 10 famous musicians who came to resent the very hits that made them stars — and why they just could not sing them anymore.

news.title: How far can a robot drive on Mars? Perseverance just broke the record

news.title: How did a tiny kitten survive stuck inside a car engine for hours?

news.title: Why did a prairie grass fire race across a Canadian military base in 30 seconds?
news.excerpt: A training exercise at Canada's CFB Wainwright turned deadly when a grass fire, fanned by strong winds, raced nearly a kilometre in under a minute — too fast for anyone to run.

news.title: How did a lost dog survive a whole month alone in Yellowstone — with grizzly bears and wolves nearby?
news.excerpt: A 10-year-old Jack Russell terrier named Luna went missing from a cabin in Yellowstone and survived more than a month on her own — crossing roads, slipping into lodges through automatic doors, and dodging predators before volunteers rescued her with a live trap baited with her family's shirt.

news.title: Japan's MMX Craft Blasts Off for Mars to Grab Phobos Dust

news.title: How did scientists learn to turn brain cells on and off with light? They won the 2026 Nobel Prize
news.excerpt: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to scientists who figured out how a tiny green alga's light sensor could let us flip brain cells on and off with a flash of light — and even help restore vision.

news.title: How does a bird that flies thousands of miles generate thrust on the way UP?

news.title: Why does Mozambique's 'butterfly forest' teem with 200 species found nowhere else?

news.title: How 99-Year-Old Helga Duffy Became the World's Oldest Wing-Walker

news.title: Why do nightjars sacrifice speed for the longest migration trick in the sky?
