news.title: Mosasaurs: the fast, sneaky hunters of the ancient seas
news.excerpt: While dinosaurs ruled the land, bus-sized mosasaurs hunted the ocean. New physics models show they did it with sudden, sneaky bursts of speed.

news.title: What was the chunkiest prehistoric squid? A 160-million-year-old 'squid butt' found in Wyoming
news.excerpt: Paleontologists have found the chunkiest belemnite ever — an ancient squid relative whose barrel-shaped fossil was as wide as it was long, hiding in Wyoming's rocks for 160 million years.

news.title: Why Saving One Misty Mountain Lets 200 Kinds of Butterflies Stay Home
news.excerpt: Mozambique protected a misty forest on Mount Mabu so the 200+ butterfly species that live there can keep calling it home.

news.title: How a Sloth Bear Named Odum Went From Street Performer to Sanctuary Star
news.excerpt: Odum was a dancing bear on Indian streets, named by Julia Roberts in 2009. 17 years later he's still the joy of his rescue center.

news.title: A simple touch can bring dying corals back to life in 7 weeks
news.excerpt: Scientists found that a bleached, whitening coral can fully recover if it simply touches a healthy coral from the same family. It is the fastest comeback from bleaching ever recorded.

news.title: Why do some lakes look like they broke nature's rules? Meet 10 of the strangest
news.excerpt: Most lakes are just water in a hole. But some glow pink, bubble with methane, burn with underground heat, or even float on the seafloor. Here are 10 real lakes that look like nature hit the weird button.

news.title: Can scientists turn 80-year-old cells back into 20-year-old ones?
news.excerpt: German researchers reprogrammed blood cells from an 80-year-old person straight into brain stem cells, and the cells' molecular age clock reset from 80 down to under 20.

news.title: How does a dog sniff out an invisible sea invader called 'sea vomit'?
news.excerpt: A Labrador named Sgiath learned to sniff out a slimy, orange invader on the seafloor — and save the day for native sea creatures.

news.title: Why is NASA hunting for caves to build a Moon base?
news.excerpt: Before anyone can live on the Moon, NASA wants to find underground caves, hidden ice, and safe ground. Three new missions are going to scout the way.

news.title: Can a world 20 light-years away have weather?
news.excerpt: NASA's Webb telescope watched a wild world 20 light-years away and found its stormy skies follow surprisingly tidy rules — three repeating weather patterns, not total chaos.

news.title: Can a crayfish get bigger than 'Crawzilla'?
news.excerpt: A friendly rivalry over one giant Kentucky crayfish sent scientists on a nationwide hunt — and the real record-holder turned up hiding in a museum drawer.

news.title: A 12-foot shark got stuck in a city canal — and the internet made it famous
news.excerpt: A bronze whaler shark chased its lunch into a canal in South Korea and could not find its way out. Then 600,000 people came to wave.

news.title: NASA's SPHEREx finds 'goth' brown dwarfs with stormy, colorful skies
news.excerpt: NASA's SPHEREx space telescope looked at 37 lonely 'failed stars' called brown dwarfs and discovered they have moody, goth-like atmospheres packed with water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and methane — all shifting across a temperature range from 4,000 to -10 degrees Fahrenheit.

news.title: Eight orangutans go home: a forest waited for them
news.excerpt: After wildfires destroyed much of their jungle this summer, eight orangutans were rescued, cared for, and driven back to a safe forest. It was the first release since the fires began — and the news made a lot of people happy.

news.title: Why did a bear walk into a bakery at a farmers market?
news.excerpt: A hungry black bear strolled straight past the shoppers at an Aspen market and made a beeline for the bread booth — and stayed, they say, for a snack and a nap.

news.title: Why are owls nesting in a Manhattan water tower?
news.excerpt: A family of barn owls moved onto a rooftop water tower in the heart of New York City — the first barn owl nest anyone can remember in Manhattan.

news.title: Why Do Blueberries Make Your Brain Happy? The Gut-Brain-Berry Link
news.excerpt: A small study found that older adults who ate blueberries every day for three months had fewer sad-mood feelings and friendlier gut bacteria than those who ate a placebo. The fruit is packed with color-powered plant chemicals that may help the gut and brain chat better.

news.title: Why is NASA's $4.3 billion telescope already beating expectations in space?
news.excerpt: Weeks after launching on August 30, NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is already delivering images nearly 30% sharper than pre-launch predictions — thanks to engineers tweaking mirrors by a sliver thinner than a human hair.

news.title: Look up: October's sky has a meteor shower
news.excerpt: NASA's monthly sky guide says the Orionid meteor shower lights up this month — here is how to watch it with no telescope at all.

news.title: A telescope named after 'the mother of Hubble
news.excerpt: NASA's newest space telescope made TIME's list of the best inventions of 2026 — and it carries the name of a woman who fought to be in astronomy at all.

news.title: What if a road only one atom high could carry tiny cars?
news.excerpt: Scientists found that atomic steps just one atom tall can act like invisible rails, guiding quantum whirlpools in superconductors more than 1,000 times more easily than any other path. It is a tiny shortcut that could one day make electricity cables loss-free.

news.title: Five cheetah cubs, one very busy camera
news.excerpt: Five cheetah cubs were born at the Smithsonian's conservation park — and you can watch all of them, around the clock, on a livestream.
